ruleset.notes: Baseline ruleset: no towers, walls, siege, upkeep or surrender. Commanders at default reasoning effort.

hypothesis: Two identical models, two opposed opening doctrines: does the persona paragraph alone decide the match?

verdicts.claim: Identical models given different doctrine paragraphs play differently
verdicts.note: Referee: 'identical intelligence, and the opening doctrine decided everything'.

verdicts.claim: A game with no fortification tools is decided by the first attack
verdicts.note: Blue went from 23 units to zero between t=306 and t=336 with no defensive option.

lessons: With no fortification in the ruleset, the rush is not a strategy — it is the only strategy.
Blue died holding 1150 gold and 330 lumber: unspent resources are a loss condition.
The hard worker cap at 10 turned surplus economy straight into army for Red.

ruleset.notes: Added Tower (requires Barracks), Wall, the declarative catalog and `unlocked`. First round with commanders at low reasoning effort. No siege units existed yet.

hypothesis: Now that towers and walls exist, can fortification beat the rush?

verdicts.claim: Fortification beats the rush
verdicts.note: The match never produced a verdict: the simulator stopped feeding the bridge at t=3656 with game_over still null.

verdicts.claim: Without siege, defence deadlocks the game
verdicts.note: Archers (range 14) cannot engage towers (range 16); two frontal assaults cost Blue ~35 units for 5 towers. 48 game-minutes, no result.

verdicts.claim: Nothing in this game can be repaired, so towers can be out-dueled passively
verdicts.note: Blue's 'tower creep' worked — found roughly twenty minutes too late.

lessons: Round one: rush wins because defence doesn't exist. Round two: defence deadlocks the game for 48 minutes because siege doesn't exist.
A counter that outranges its target by 2 is not a counter.
Tempo took Red to the doorstep; with no economy it could not walk through — 16 towers built out of an unusable 4000g bank.

ruleset.notes: Added upkeep, mines halved 10000->5000, health regen, Catapult and Workshop, surrender, doctrine templates, reactive Defend posture, worker auto-rebalance. Time limits explicitly rejected.

hypothesis: What do upkeep and halved mines do to the fortress meta?

result.duration_note: AAR says 'game-minute 13'; no logged second count survives.

verdicts.claim: Scarcity plus upkeep forces a decision without a time limit
verdicts.note: The last mine on the map became the battlefield; the game ended at ~13 minutes.

verdicts.claim: Siege breaks the fortress
verdicts.note: Catapults outrange towers by 4. Nine catapults deleted 19 units, two towers, the Town Hall and the hero in fifteen seconds.

lessons: Incentives, not rules: mines that run dry end games that a clock would only interrupt.
Greed needs a shell around it — every expansion Blue placed died before its first tower finished.
A consolidated deathball arriving at the last mine is what 'the map demands a fight' looks like.

ruleset.notes: Added the ability framework, Raider (ungated), Priestess, Militia / CallToArms, Shop with Potion and TownPortal.

hypothesis: The richest ruleset yet — with abilities, items and a shop, does any of the new content appear in a winner's after-action report?

verdicts.claim: Ungated cavalry is a degenerate opening
verdicts.note: Five Raiders killed all fourteen of Blue's workers in sixteen seconds (t=212-228). Fastest match of the series; Red lost one unit all game.

verdicts.claim: New content gets used
verdicts.note: Doctrine templates and the Raider decided the round — but nobody picked the Priestess, which is the acceptance test failing for her.

lessons: Greed is a bet that the first punch lands late. This round Blue paid nothing and lost everything.
A doctrine template that sets focus-fire to 'Worker first' makes the raid self-executing — the engine did the micro.
Preserve strategies, relocate them: the Raider was gated behind the Workshop rather than deleted.

ruleset.notes: The round-4 patch: Raider now requires a Workshop. Otherwise identical to r4.

hypothesis: With the Raider gated behind a Workshop, can patience win on this ruleset at all?

result.duration_note: Blue's AAR gives t~1167s; Red surrendered at t~1163.

verdicts.claim: Patience cannot win on this ruleset
verdicts.note: First boomer win of the series, and it was not close: 41 attackers broken in twelve seconds of combat.

verdicts.claim: Tower coverage is decoration
verdicts.note: Blue refused the open field and fought inside a four-tower crossfire with CallToArms militia. 'Tower coverage is doctrine, not decoration.'

lessons: A doomstack isn't a doomstack if it walks at three different speeds — the cohesion finding.
Refusing the open field is a decision, not passivity: choose the ground and the counter-triangle does the rest.
Hero XP compounds inside a won fight — Blue's hero went level 1 to 5 in nine seconds.

ruleset.notes: Added bounty caches: first at 2:30, every 90s thereafter, 75s lifetime, 225 gold growing 0.5/s, capped at 600.

hypothesis: Do contested neutral bounty caches cure mutual turtling?

verdicts.claim: Contested caches cure turtling
verdicts.note: The biggest asterisk of the series: Blue conceded on the owner's instruction while its position was winning. The ending was not play.

verdicts.claim: A cache is won by the squad, not the detachment
verdicts.note: Blue: 'Every cache I won, I won with the whole squad walking onto it. Every one I lost, I lost by sending 2 units.'

lessons: Every cache I won, I won with the whole squad walking onto it; every one I lost, I lost by sending two units.
A round that ends by instruction rather than by play answers nothing — record the asterisk or the series lies.

ruleset.notes: Added anti-idle autonomy (every army unit auto-enrols in squad 0, `forage` posture) and bridge_wait.py event pacing for the commanders.

hypothesis: Does the anti-idle autonomy layer change the texture of a match?

result.duration_note: Red surrendered at t=3444s; Blue logged the concession at t=3516.

verdicts.claim: Anti-idle autonomy changes the texture of a match
verdicts.note: Armies acted continuously between commander cycles; the match ran 57 game-minutes and was decided by the bounty war, not by idleness.

verdicts.claim: A latched retreat policy is safe
verdicts.note: It froze Blue's entire army for roughly five minutes (t=1801-2317) and cost three 600g bounties, uncollected. Drove retreat auto-recovery.

lessons: Gold in the bank when the mines are dying is a wasted army.
Red fumbled the window: it pulled back to regroup with 1400g banked instead of re-committing.
Roughly 8-10 bounties at 600g each decided the round — the map's economy, not the armies, was the battlefield.

ruleset.notes: Added cohesive advance (COHESION_SPREAD 14), STANDOFF_MARGIN (range-2), BOUNTY_CLAIM_RADIUS 6.0, retreat auto-recovery.

hypothesis: Does the full counter-triangle — cohesion, standoff, retreat recovery — actually function in a match?

result.duration_note: Conflicting accounts: Red's AAR says it surrendered at t~3700; the referee and Blue record a raze at t~3883. The raze is the engine's own ending, so it is the one recorded.

verdicts.claim: The counter-triangle functions
verdicts.note: First outright annihilation of the series; Blue consolidated 44 units into one squad and broke Red completely for the loss of 18 archers.

verdicts.claim: A supply-capped team has no gold sink but towers
verdicts.note: With mines exhausted and ~4900g/4200l banked against the hard 100-supply cap, Blue dumped the surplus into 25 towers, which cost no supply. Filed as wc3clone-5bw; the owner ruled it answered by siege, not by a lever.

lessons: The boomer creed held: bank long, then commit once, completely.
Red fed three armies into the same mistake and never once fought next to its own towers.
The R8 tower-overflow: surplus gold becomes towers because towers are the only supply-free sink.
A forage squad moving at catapult speed cannot contest caches against raiders that snipe them in 4-8 seconds.

ruleset.notes: First commander match on `crossings` and under the v2 ruleset: production-only victory, uncapped bounties, fog of war, tier ladder T1-T3, Sorcerer/Spearman/Knight/Gryphon, tiered shop, intent_compile.py. Windowed and spectated.

hypothesis: Do the v2 rules — fog of war, the T1-T3 tier ladder, production-only victory and 3500-gold mines — land matches in the 10-20 minute target?

verdicts.claim: The v2 ruleset hits the 10-20 minute pacing target
verdicts.note: 5:24 — the match ended before tier 2 existed. Both AARs blamed mines drying at minute 4-5 under saturation. Bead wc3clone-wwl.

verdicts.claim: The winner can tell which victory they got
verdicts.note: Red: 'the win triggered with their Keep and Workshop alive, so I cannot tell from the feed whether I met the raze condition or they conceded.' This is why GameOverReason exists (shared.rs) — the field did not exist when this round was played, so the ending is recorded as unknown.

verdicts.claim: Fog makes scouting a build-order item
verdicts.note: Red's foraging squad found Blue's remote expansion at t=249 by walking onto it; Blue never found Red's army until it arrived.

lessons: Mine depletion outruns the tech ladder: 3500 gold against ~11 workers is about four minutes.
A ford does not defend itself — a remote expansion 130 units from the main split army from base and hero from army.
Fog makes scouting a build-order item, not a luxury.
Placement failures must say what they need: 'site is blocked for TownHall' with no clearance number cost both commanders 20+ seconds of guessing.

ruleset.notes: One lever changed from r9: MINE_GOLD 3500->5000 (commit c8be188). The owner chose restoring the pre-patch mine size over cheapening T2 or nerfing saturation. Everything else as r9.

hypothesis: Does the rusher line still win with 40% more gold in the ground, and do commanders reach T2/T3 when the economy allows?

verdicts.claim: The rusher line still wins with 5000-gold mines
verdicts.note: Red won at 9:21 — but 'as a T2 timing push rather than a T1 dive'. Series: Rusher 6, Boomer 3, 1 draw.

verdicts.claim: More gold buys a real mid-game
verdicts.note: 9:21 against r9's 5:24, with both creeds fielding full T2: Keep at 3:30-4:00, research, Sanctums, Sorcerers, expansions, ford towers. Bead wc3clone-2hs.

verdicts.claim: More gold gets commanders to T3
verdicts.note: Castle, Knights and Gryphons were never reached — not for want of gold (Red finished on 1539g, peaked at 2900) but because lumber was the hard cap all game.

lessons: The economy clock was outrunning the tech ladder; raising mine gold moved the ceiling without touching the ladder.
Lumber, not gold, is what actually gates tier 3.
The forage posture walked a whole squad into the enemy base at 4:50 and fed six Footmen to a tower piecemeal.
One tower is not a fortification; army split is instantly fatal and the game gives no warning.
Blue surrendered holding 2195 gold and 370 lumber: boom-into-tech does not beat tempo here yet.

ruleset.notes: First round recorded by tools/arena_run.py rather than by hand. Scripted mirror: both sides driven by ai.rs, no commander seats, no probe knobs.

hypothesis: Under the v2 ruleset on crossings, does a scripted mirror still reach a decisive ending inside the 10-20 minute pacing target?

verdicts.claim: A scripted mirror under the v2 ruleset reaches a decisive ending inside the 10-20 minute pacing target
verdicts.note: 11:13 game time, razed, no time cap hit — and an identical earlier run of this same configuration ended 14:11. Both are inside the target, which is the claim; neither is a repeatable number.

lessons: The world seed is fixed (MAP_SEED) but the match is not: two runs of this identical configuration gave different winners and lengths (Claude 11:13, Human 14:11). A single round is evidence about a ruleset, never a measurement of it.
The scripted mirror on crossings runs longer than the commander rounds did (11:13 and 14:11 against r10's 9:21): the script banks where a commander commits.

hypothesis: with deliberate lumber allocation, does T3 arrive inside a 10-20min game — and does boom-into-tech beat tempo under targeted Slow?

verdicts.claim: Boom-into-tech beats tempo under targeted Slow
verdicts.note: Boomer lost a 4th straight (surrender 9:27, army 9 vs 16 at the decisive 6:34-6:44 fight): tech ate the gold that should have been army. Targeted Slow was a non-event on BOTH sides — casters finished after the decisive engagement; it is a timing problem, not a targeting problem.

verdicts.claim: T3 arrives inside a 10-20min game with deliberate lumber allocation
verdicts.note: Both sides: Blue Castle 6:05 (9g/5l split, ~1000l ladder paid, 1050l spare), Red Castle 7:02 (3-of-7 workers on trees, ~1900l earned). Lumber was allocation, not pricing — no balance change needed.

lessons: The binding constraint moved again: gold-to-army conversion timing (Red idle 909g, Blue's second production building never made line units). Whoever converts bank to bodies before the first big fight wins; tech pays only if you survive it.
Sorcerer timing: at current tempo, casters completed after the decisive fight in both seats. If Slow should matter, it must be reachable before ~6:00 or fights must come later.

ruleset.notes: v3 race 2: WC3_RACE_RED=horde, first arena round with a second roster

hypothesis: does the Horde roster reach decisive games in the pacing band vs Kingdom?

verdicts.claim: The Horde roster reaches a decisive game against the Kingdom inside the pacing band
verdicts.note: Razed win at 797s (13:17), inside the 10-20min band the series has been tuning toward. The Horde fielded a real roster rather than a fallback line: 6 Grunt, 6 Headhunter, 3 Impaler, 2 Demolisher, 4 Shaman and both hero classes.

lessons: A second race is decisive out of the box only once its LINE unit is priced as a floor: the scripted commander degrades to the roster's Line unit when it cannot afford its pick, so a line unit that is the most expensive body on the card turns a reserve squeeze into a total production stall. Measured before the fix: 1343 banked gold, 8 army units, against 28.

ruleset.notes: v3 race 2: WC3_RACE_RED=horde on crossings

hypothesis: does the Horde roster reach decisive games in the pacing band vs Kingdom, on the chokepoint map?

verdicts.claim: The Horde stays decisive on the chokepoint map, where its lack of a Wall might have cost it the ford
verdicts.note: Razed win at 949s. The Horde has no Barrier building by design, so it never contests the ford with walls the way the Kingdom does; it won anyway, which says the ford fortification is a Kingdom option rather than a requirement.

lessons: Roster asymmetry survives a chokepoint map: the race with fewer buildings does not need the fortification vocabulary the other race has, because the ford is a place you can also just take.

ruleset.notes: v3 race 2 re-merge: same config as r13, re-run on the merged binary

hypothesis: after jem/intel/plans/territory land, does the Horde still reach decisive games vs Kingdom — and does it still win any?

verdicts.claim: The Horde still wins sometimes on the open map
verdicts.note: It now loses from both seats at every seed tested on open; its wins survive only on crossings. See r16.

verdicts.claim: The Horde still reaches a decisive game after the merge
verdicts.note: Razed at 318.6s — decisive, but the Horde is the one razed. Pre-merge the same config was a Horde win at 797s.

lessons: Balancing a second race against a scripted commander is balancing against a MOVING baseline: jem/intel/plans/territory changed how the AI fights, and a roster tuned to 7-of-12 before the merge came out 3-of-12 after it, with no content change at all. Race balance findings expire when the opponent's script does.

ruleset.notes: v3 race 2 re-merge: same config as r14, re-run on the merged binary

hypothesis: on the chokepoint map, does the Horde still take a decisive win after the four branches land?

verdicts.claim: The Horde still takes decisive wins on the chokepoint map after the merge
verdicts.note: Razed win at 907.1s, and it swept all three crossings seeds from the red seat with a real roster on the field (3 Grunt, 2 Headhunter, 1 Impaler, 6 Demolisher, 3 Shaman, both heroes).

lessons: The Horde's surviving edge is the chokepoint map, where its Demolisher line gets to work behind a held ford; on open ground it is out-tempoed before its one production building can answer. That is a defensible racial shape, but it is narrower than the pre-merge measurement claimed.

hypothesis: does the Horde hold up under commander play against the Kingdom — and do the new vocabularies (triggers/plans/regions/intel) show up in winning play?

verdicts.claim: The Horde holds up under commander play
verdicts.note: First commander game: Horde won by raze at 7:15 with a single 21-unit equal-gold push, hero-less. The scripted 3/12 regression does not reflect commander play — 1qp's retune should target scripted cadence, not roster numbers, on this evidence.

verdicts.claim: The new vocabularies carry weight in winning play
verdicts.note: Red: one plan_set executed the entire opening in ~2s of engine time; unit_count and enemy_hero_down triggers launched and re-aimed the winning attack with zero polling. Blue: all five armed triggers fired on exactly the right conditions — the loss was commander attention, not vocabulary failure.

lessons: Headhunter lumber pricing is the cross-race asymmetry that decided the composition war: cheaper-lumber ranged let the Horde mass a ranged core while the Kingdom sat on 400 idle lumber gold-starved. Balance watch.

A blocked plan step's error spam drove Blue into a ~100s bridge_wait coma that decided the game — blocked-step errors need rate-limiting or a single sticky status line instead of repeats. UX bead candidate.

hypothesis: r17 rematch with the fire-hose dead: does the Kingdom boomer hold up against the Horde when blocked plans are edges, bridge_wait stays quiet through retries, and supply_capped is armable?

verdicts.claim: The Kingdom boomer holds up once the fire-hose is dead
verdicts.note: Blue won by Red's surrender at 7:10 — both WarCamps razed, 18 Archers standing in the Horde base. The r17 failure mode never recurred: one wait/view/decision per cycle, recipe-7 supply valve fired 6x unattended, peak idle gold ~560 for one cycle vs r17's 2280. First boomer win since round 8.

lessons: Both seats' standing machinery now executes flawlessly — r18 was decided entirely by judgment: Red stopped scouting at 2:46, over-teched (Fortress 3:08, both researches by 5:25, army of 13), and keyed its offensive trigger on its own tech (4 Shamans) instead of relative strength, firing after the army it measured was dead. The engine does the fast work; the player's choices decide. That is THESIS.md's win condition, observed.

Trigger predicate choice is the new skill expression: Blue's unit_count>=10 launched a war-winning timing attack; Red's 4-Shaman condition measured the wrong thing entirely. Same vocabulary, opposite outcomes — the language is neutral, the sentences are not.

Heroes are being rationally skipped at 7-minute tempo: r17's winner, r18's winner, AND r18's loser all fought hero-less. 400g/100l with XP payoff over 10+ minutes doesn't fit games that resolve at ~7 — Blue queued a Hero at 3:27 and cancelled it at 4:54 to buy three line units mid-push. Hero economics were tuned for the 13-60min era. Balance candidate: cheaper first hero, faster XP, or accept heroes as long-game content.

Queue priority has exactly one lever: cancellation. No reorder, no train-when-affordable-without-blocking, no looping production (plans are once-through; only unit_count >= exists, not <). Blue's complaint verbatim: production should be 'a policy like everything else'. Post-v3 candidate: production policy verb (maintain N of kind) — which would also retire the every-Nth composition hacks in ai.rs.

hypothesis: the classic mirror with the full vocabulary: does the rusher still beat the boomer when both wield triggers/plans/regions/intel — and does either commander judge a hero worth 400g at this tempo?

verdicts.claim: Commanders judge a hero worth 400g at this tempo
verdicts.note: Both skipped deliberately with stated reasoning: Red on principle (three Footmen NOW), Blue bought a third Barracks instead — 'reinforcement rate, not a champion, is what broke their timing attack.' Five straight hero-less winners. The s61 hero-economics bead now has its answer: at current tempo the rational hero count is zero.

verdicts.claim: The rusher still beats the boomer in the full-vocabulary mirror
verdicts.note: Boomer won at 6:01 with ZERO buildings lost — faster than any rush ever landed. Second straight boomer win. The vocabulary rewards standing production machinery (3 Barracks, 6 unattended farms, region-aimed defense, Archer>=15 commit trigger) over first-punch tempo: Red's 2:41 seven-archer push died in 16s and a hero-less rush has no second act. Series: Rusher 7, Boomer 5, 1 draw — momentum flipped.

lessons: The trigger vocabulary cannot express RELATIVE strength — both r18's and r19's losers keyed commit triggers to absolute own-side counts (4 Shamans; Archer>=6) because 'when my army outnumbers their last-seen army' is unspellable. The intel ledger holds both numbers; no predicate compares them. Comparative predicates (army_advantage{ratio}) are the missing sentence — candidate for the NL/predicate-composition bead.

hypothesis: the new-rules mirror: with a symmetric t=0 start and free heroes (400g/100l only on death), do champions finally take the field — and does keeping them alive decide the round?

verdicts.claim: Free heroes take the field
verdicts.note: All three heroes fielded across both seats (Red Champion t=25; Blue Champion + Priestess at Keep) after five straight hero-less rounds. The inversion works: zero fielding cost ended the rational skip immediately.

verdicts.claim: Keeping the hero alive decides the round
verdicts.note: Blue preserved both heroes all match (never below 83%) and they personally killed the TownHall — the bill never came due because Blue played as if it might. Red's Champion died at t=320, pulled into five attackers by its own defend posture faster than a poll cycle could react. Hero preservation was the round's visible skill gap, exactly as the inversion intended.

lessons: The held-at-t=0 window is powerful and double-edged: Blue armed its entire winning opening in 94s of planning (Barracks at t=1, hero at t=2); Red used the same window to arm a plan that named its three GOLD workers as builders and mined nothing for 53 seconds. Symmetric time, asymmetric quality — which is the design working, but plan authoring needs a builder-selection footgun guard (prefer idle/non-mining workers).

Doctrine treats a hero as just another squad member: Red's leash/defend posture yanked its Champion into a five-unit ball — the posture executor has no concept of a unit whose death costs 400g. Hero-exception rungs are a concrete argument for the held priority-stacks bead (uxs): 'squad defends home UNLESS I am the hero and outnumbered'. Also: the rusher creed has now died the same death twice (committed push into an assembled ball at the enemy hall — r19, r20); the creed needs a strength-comparison predicate (43b) more than any other player.

sonnet vs sonnet rematch: does the boomer adapt after reading r21 AARs?
fable vs fable: play the match, then describe how to prioritize the decision space for smaller commanders
